## The SCORE replications {#the-score-replications .smaller}

::: {.fs-75}
| Replication | New data | Respondents | Coefficient | *t* |
|:----------|:------------------------------------|--:|--:|--:|
| osf.io/rpumq | ESS round 5 (2010), 13 of the 16 countries, two-level model, post-stratification weights | `r fmt_n(mark_of("SCORE_1634", "n"))` | `r fmt_num(mark_of("SCORE_1634", "b"), 3)` | `r fmt_num(mark_of("SCORE_1634", "statistic"), 2)` |
| osf.io/e48gd, data-analytic | ESS rounds 5–9 (2010–2018), 72 country-rounds of the 16 countries, three-level model | `r fmt_n(mark_of("SCORE_65wm6_DAR", "n"))` | `r fmt_num(mark_of("SCORE_65wm6_DAR", "b"), 3)` | `r fmt_num(mark_of("SCORE_65wm6_DAR", "statistic"), 2)` |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Both met the criterion of SCORE, a positive coefficient that is significant at the 5% level, and both lie within 0.01 of the reproductions of the original model. The round 5 replication lost Austria and Italy, which the integrated file of the round does not hold, and Portugal, whose sample lacks household income.
:::

::: {.src}
cases/trust/data/reference_marks.csv; the reports of the replications are on the OSF.
:::

::: notes
Now we leave the original rounds behind. SCORE commissioned two replications that asked the same question of new respondents, in later rounds of the same survey. The first used round five, fielded in 2010, with a two-level model and post-stratification weights; it covers thirteen of the sixteen countries, because the integrated file of that round has no Austrian or Italian sample, and the Portuguese sample lacks household income. It found point one eight three. The second, a data-analytic replication by one of the reproduction teams, used rounds five to nine, eight years of fieldwork, with the three-level model of the paper, and found point one eight six on ninety thousand new respondents. [advance] Both met the criterion of SCORE, and both landed within a hundredth of the reproductions of the original model. The association held, at the same size, for a decade after the paper.
:::

## The three Rs on this paper {#the-three-rs-on-this-paper}

```{r}
#| label: scoreboard
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 4.6
# The SCORE dossier on the immigration-and-trust case as a three-row
# scoreboard, one row per R; the details come from
# _planning/trust/trust-facts.md and from the curve and record files.
sb <- tribble(
  ~ord, ~R,              ~verdict,                    ~detail,                                                                                                                                                                                                     ~fill,
  3,    "Reproducible?", "COEFFICIENT YES, SAMPLE NO", sprintf("no data or code from OA; two rebuilds from the ESS\nreproduce the coefficient (%s, %s) but not the sample;\nthe class reproduced 6U3LL exactly", fmt_num(mark_of("SCORE_jp7tr", "b"), 3), fmt_num(mark_of("SCORE_65wm6", "b"), 3)), orange,
  2,    "Robust?",       "THE ANALYSTS AGREE 5–0",     sprintf("%d specifications, all positive and significant,\n%s to %s points; all five analysts found\nevidence for the claim, from %s to %s", nrow(curve), fmt_num(min(curve$b), 3), fmt_num(max(curve$b), 3), fmt_num(min(analysts$b_refit), 3), fmt_num(max(analysts$b_refit), 3)), green,
  1,    "Replicable?",   "REPLICATED TWICE",           sprintf("ESS round 5: %s (t = %s)\nESS rounds 5–9: %s (t = %s)", fmt_num(mark_of("SCORE_1634", "b"), 3), fmt_num(mark_of("SCORE_1634", "statistic"), 1), fmt_num(mark_of("SCORE_65wm6_DAR", "b"), 3), fmt_num(mark_of("SCORE_65wm6_DAR", "statistic"), 1)), green
)

ggplot(sb, aes(x = 1, y = ord)) +
  geom_tile(aes(x = 1.2, fill = fill), width = 1.34, height = 0.92, alpha = 0.14) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0.538, xend = 0.538, y = ord - 0.46, yend = ord + 0.46, colour = fill),
               linewidth = 6) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  scale_colour_identity() +
  geom_text(aes(label = R), x = 0.60, hjust = 0, vjust = 0.5, fontface = "bold",
            colour = ncl_blue, size = 8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = verdict, colour = fill, y = ord - 0.26), x = 0.60, hjust = 0, vjust = 0.5,
            fontface = "bold", size = 4.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = detail), x = 1.1, hjust = 0, vjust = 0.5, colour = "grey35", size = 4.4,
            lineheight = 0.95) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.5, 1.9)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.4, 3.6)) +

```

::: {.src}
The SCORE project of the paper: [osf.io/3ajr9](https://osf.io/3ajr9/)
:::

::: notes
Put the whole dossier together. Reproducibility: OA supplied neither data nor code, and the links in the paper no longer worked, so two SCORE teams rebuilt the data from the survey files. Both reproduced the coefficient, and neither reproduced the sample, because nobody knows how the paper reached a hundred and ten thousand respondents in every model. And you reproduced the result of 6U3LL exactly this afternoon. Robustness, on the original data, holds in the strongest sense that a curve can offer: every specification that the course judged justifiable, and every one of the five analysts, finds the association, in the same direction, significant. Only its size moves, nearly threefold. Replication on new rounds of the survey succeeded twice. So, the sample apart, this paper passes all three. That is the right moment to ask what passing them means.
:::

## Repetition and the causal reading {#repetition-and-the-causal-reading}

:::: {.none .fs-85}
::: {.fragment}
The claim passes all three Rs as far as its coefficient goes: it reproduces from rebuilt data, although the sample of the paper does not, survives every analysis on the menu, and returns in later rounds of the survey.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Every one of those repetitions compares **people interviewed once** with other people interviewed once.
:::

::: {.fragment}
So all three test the **association**. None tests the direction that the word "impact" claims.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Distrust that feeds concern, or a common cause that no model holds constant, would pass the same three tests.
:::
::::

::: notes
This is the lesson of the case, and it is the mirror image of the housing-audit case, where the claim survived every analysis of the original data and failed with new data. [advance] Here everything passes. But look at what every one of those repetitions does: it takes people interviewed once and compares them with other people interviewed once. [advance] So all three Rs test the association, and none of them tests the direction that the word impact claims. [advance] If distrust fed concern, as FQ1G7 suggested, or if some common cause that no model holds constant produced both, the reproductions would still reproduce, the curve would still be all circles, and the replications would still replicate. An association can be robust and replicable and still not be an effect. A design that could settle the direction, such as a panel that follows the same people over time, is a different study.
:::
